docs.text:
Logan Maelstrom Datasheet as part of Drowsy Driver Alarm for Team 104

Submission: Sept. 02 2026

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: This datasheet documents my subsystem for a team drowsy-driver detection and alert system. The subsystem uses a (6DoF) gyroscope/accelerometer called a BMI270 IMU, and PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano, to detect and process head movement associated with driver drowsiness.

docs.title: Project Summary
docs.text: The Drowsy Driver Alarm project combines multiple subsystems to detect signs of driver fatigue and provide appropriate alerts. My subsystem monitors head movement using the BMI270 accelerometer and gyroscope and communicates with the team's other subsystems through the microcontroller and team interface Additional information about the complete system can be found in the team report.

docs.title: My Contribution
docs.text: My primary contribution to the project is the design and documentation of the IMU subsystem. This includes integrating the BMI270 with the PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano, designing a 5 V and 3.3 V power regulation circuitry, implementing the I²C interface, providing team-interface connections, and including debugging and expansion features. I also developed a subsystem schematic for the IMU and selected the supporting components required for reliable operation. * Block Diagram: Provides an overview of the subsystem and its connections. * Component Selection: Documents the major components and the reasoning behind their use. * BOM: Lists the components required to construct the subsystem. * Schematic: Provides the complete electrical design and downloadable design files. * Power Budget: Documents the subsystem's expected power requirements. Together, these sections provide the information needed to understand, review, and continue development of my portion of the overall team system.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The purpose of this block diagram is to provide a clear overview of the system’s electrical connections and how the major components interact. The system is powered by a 9 V unregulated source, which is stepped down through 5 V and 3.3 V regulators to provide the required power levels for the different components. A PIC18F57Q43 microcontroller serves as the main controller, receiving sensor data from the BMI270 through SDA and SCL communication lines. The BMI270 is an accelerometer and gyro sensor, serving as a useful component that can sense head movements related to drowsiness while driving. The microcontroller also interfaces with components such as the debug LED and button, as well as three team connectors that provide digital and analog signals. Overall, the diagram helps show the system’s power distribution, sensor connections, control signals, and interfaces between different parts of the project.

docs.title: Component Selection
docs.text:
6-Axis Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU)

  1. BMI323 Surface-Mount Accelerometer/Gyroscope/Temperature (6 axis)

    • $3.91/each
    • link to product
    Pros Cons Low power consumption Tiny 14-pin LGA package Compatible with 3.3V rail More features than our project application may require Supports I²C Requires software/configuration work Small package No integrated magnetometer Built-in motion/orientation detection Wide programmable measurement ranges

  2. BMI270 Surface-Mount Accelerometer/Gyroscope/Temperature (6 axis)

    • $4.23/each
    • Link to product
    Pros Cons Low power consumption More expensive than BMI323 Compatable with 3.3V rail Tiny 14-pin LGA package is difficult to solder/prototype Supports I²C communication Many wearable features aren't useful for the specific Drowsy Driver Alarm project Designed specifically for wearable applications Requires software/configuration to work Small size/footprint (2.5mm x 3.0mm) Built-in motion detection features

  3. LSM6DSMTR Surface-Mount Accelerometer/Gyroscope/Temperature (6 axis)

    • $4.55/each
    • Link to product
    Pros Cons Low power consumption More expensive than both previous examples Compatible with 3.3V rail Tiny 14-pin LGA package is difficult to solder/prototype Supports I²C communication Older-generation IMU design Built-in tilt detection and significant motion detection No I3C interface High mechanical-shock robustness OIS/EIS features are unnecessary for our Drowsy Driver Alarm project Dedicated motion interrupts LGA package is difficult to prototype with

Choice: Option 2: BMI270 surface mount accelerometer/gyroscope (6 axis)

Rationale: The BMI270 was manufactured with the purpose of wearable applications, such as recognizing human/head motion, making it a striking candidate from the list. Bosch specifically designed this chip for the same purpose our project is meant to portray. the BMI270 also has on-chip any-motion, no-motion, stationary, significant-motion, and activity-change recognition, which lines up incredibly well with that our project is trying to accomplish. Overall, this is our best candidate for a fair price, and there are plenty of units in stock on DigiKey with quick shipping times.

3.3V Voltage Regulator

  1. AP2112K-3.3TRG1 Surface-Mount 3.3V LDO Linear Regulator

  • $0.28/each
  • Link to product
Pros Cons Very inexpensive 80µA quiescent current High 600mA output capacity Linear-regulator efficiency loss Low dropout voltage Limited to 6V maximum input voltage Built-in overcurrent protection Surface-mount package may be more difficult to solder Built-in overtemperature protection Fixed 3.3V output Enable/shutdown control High availability
  1. RT9080-33GJ5 Surface-Mount 3.3V LDO Linear Regulator

  • $0.28/each
  • Link to product
Pros Cons Extremely low 4µA quiescent current 5.5V maximum input voltage High 600mA output capacity Higher maximum dropout than AP2112K 75dB power-supply rejection Surface-mount package may be more difficult to solder Built-in overcurrent protection Fixed 3.3V output Built-in overtemperature protection Linear-regulator efficiency loss Enable/shutdown control High availability Very inexpensive
  1. TLV75533PDBVR Surface-Mount 3.3V LDO Linear Regulator

  • $0.42/each
  • Link to product
Pros Cons Low 31µA quiescent current Lower 500mA capacity than other candidates Low 238mV maximum dropout Higher quiescent current than RT9080 Built-in overcurrent protection 5.5V maximum input Built-in overtemperature protection Fixed 3.3V output Wide -40°C to 125°C operating range Linear-regulator efficiency loss Compact SOT-23-5 package High availability

Choice: Option 2: RT9080-33GJ5 Surface-Mount 3.3V LDO Linear Regulator

Rationale: The RT9080-33GJ5 by Richtek has the lowest quiescent current of the candidates, being 4µA. Additionally, it still gives 600mA of maximum output current and is very affordable. Low power consumption is important for the Drowsy Driver Alarm project since the product is intended to be wearable. This LDO also provides exceptional protections built-in, such as overcurrent and overtemperature protection. Although its maximum input voltage is lower than other candidates like the AP2112K, this isn't a signifcant trade-off since the RT9080 can be powered by the system's 5V rail. Overall, this inexpensive LDO is exceptionally capable for our product's needs.

5V Voltage Regulator

  1. L7805ACV-DG Through-Hole 5V Linear Regulator

  • $1.21/each
  • Link to product
Pros Cons High 1.5A output capacity High 6mA quiescent current Easy-to-solder through-hole package Poor efficiency for 9V → 5V conversion Very simple regulator circuit Can generate significant heat at higher loads Built-in short-circuit protection Large TO-220 package Built-in overtemperature protection Approximately 2V dropout at 1A 35 V maximum input provides large safety margin Fixed 5V output Good current availability
  1. LM2575MX-5.0/NOPB Surface-Mount 5V Buck (Switching) Regulator

  • $3.09/each
  • Link to product
Pros Cons More efficient than linear regulators Requires external inductor and capacitors Wide 4–40 V input range Large 24-pin SOIC package High 1 A output capacity Only 52kHz switching frequency Built-in overcurrent protection More complex PCB design than linear regulator Enable/shutdown control Switching can introduce electrical noise Reduced heat generation vs. linear regulator More expensive than L7805ACV-DG Fixed 5V output simplifies configuration Lower output capacity than LMR43620R5RPER
  1. LMR43620R5RPER Surface-Mount 5V Buck (Switching) Regulator

  • $2.27/each
  • Link to product
Pros Cons High 2A output capacity Much more expensive High efficiency compared with linear regulators Requires external inductor and capacitors Extremely low 1.3µA quiescent current More complex PCB layout Wide 3–36V input range Tiny VQFN package is more difficult to hand solder Reduced heat generation Switching regulator can introduce electrical noise Compact 2mm × 2mm package More complex than necessary for light loads Built-in overcurrent protection Wide −40°C to 150°C operating range

Choice: Option 3: LMR43620R5RPER Surface-Mount 5V Buck (Switching) Regulator

Rationale: The LMR43620R5RPER by Texas Instruments is selected because its high efficiency and low power consumption make it the best candidate for our Drowsy Driver Alarm. Unlike the L7805ACV-DG linear regulator, the LMR43620 uses a buck switching design, allowing a 9V input to be stepped down to 5V with significantly less energy being wasted as heat. This is especially beneficial for our wearable design, where excessive heat and unnecessary power consumption should be minimized. The LMR43620 also provides up to 2A of output current, giving our circuit plenty of current capacity, while its small 2mm × 2mm package minimizes PCB space. Although it is more expensive and requires additional external components, its efficiency, low 1.3µA quiescent current, compact size, and reduced heat generation make these tradeoffs worthwhile for our application.

9V External Power Source

  1. Microchip AC002014 - 9V External Power Supply, 800mA

  • $25.49/each
  • Link to product
Pros Cons Provides required 9V output Most expensive (per amp) of the three power-supply candidates Sufficient 800mA output capacity Limited to 800mA maximum output International 110–220 VAC input Lower 7.2W capacity Interchangeable AC plug blades 2.5mm ID plug requires matching barrel jack Standard center-positive barrel connector Less current headroom for future additions Commercial Class II wall supply Currently in stock
  1. UNIIVE UV313-0913 9V External Power Supply

  • $17.40/each
  • Link to product
Pros Cons Lowest price of the three candidates Lower output capacity than 2.2A Bel Power Solutions candidate Higher 1.3A output capacity Fixed US-style AC plug Universal 100–240 VAC input No interchangeable AC plug blades 82.96% efficiency 2.1mm ID requires matching barrel jack Low 100mW no-load consumption Limited 0–40°C operating range Safety approvals: CB, CE, cULus, FCC Long 1.5m output cable Currently in stock
  1. Bel Power Solutions SMI18-9-V-P6R

  • $30.27/each
  • Link to product
Pros Cons Highest 2.2A output capacity Highest overall purchase price of all candidates High 20W output power More power capacity than project likely requires Universal 90–264 VAC input Larger/heavier power adapter Interchangeable AC plug blades 2.5mm ID requires matching barrel jack Level VI energy efficiency Limited 0–40°C operating range Low 100mW no-load consumption Right-angle barrel plug may constrain enclosure layout Long 1.5m output cable Extensive international safety approvals

Choice: Option 2: UNIIVE UV313-0913 9V External Power Supply

Rationale: The UV313-0913 was selected because it provides the best balance of output capacity, price, efficiency, and availability for our Drowsy Driver Alarm project. Its 1.3A output provides more current headroom than the 800mA Microchip supply while costing significantly less. Although the Bel Power Solutions supply can provide 2.2A, that additional capacity is likely unnecessary for our system and comes at a considerably higher price. The UV313-0913 also supports universal 100–240 VAC input, has multiple safety certifications, and has low no-load power consumption. Overall, it provides sufficient power for the system without paying for unnecessary excess capacity.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This schematic is designed to utilize the embedded 6-axis IMU to detect head movements (rotation and acceleration) and send signals to the Curiosity Nano for the microcontroller to discern if the drowsy driver alarm should be deployed or not. The system contains voltage regulators to step down 9V to 5V to power the Curiosity Nano, and 5V to 3.3V to power the IMU.

[!NOTE] The schematic image should be displayed below. If it's not shown, the schematic PDF can be downloaded and opened at the bottom of this page.
